passage: I sit next to Nilesh in the reading hall, so I noticed the sheet. Every Sunday he pulls out a page with two columns, one for targets and one for what actually happened: attendance, weekly test marks. I asked once, and he said it was so he doesn't fool himself. For three weeks his marks in thermodynamics stayed low while the other subjects moved up. Then on the third Sunday he crossed out "solo study" and wrote "group with Sabina and Tarun". By the next Sunday he was in the study room with two others, arguing over one derivation. I cannot say what he felt. I only saw the sheet change, and his tests improve. — Santosh

qa.q: Which subject stayed low for three weeks?
qa.a: Thermodynamics stayed low for three weeks.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have felt on the third Sunday, judging by what Santosh saw?
qa.a: Nilesh may have felt determined and a little frustrated, since he crossed out solo study and made a change, though Santosh admits not knowing for sure.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Nilesh try if the group also stalls, and why?
qa.a: Nilesh could ask the thermodynamics teacher for the weak topics, because a group shares confusion but a teacher can correct it.

qa.q: How might Sabina see Nilesh joining the group?
qa.a: Sabina gains a new member who argues over derivations from the first week, which could make the group livelier, though the passage does not show Sabina's view directly.

grounding: Shows weekly comparison of attendance and scores with targets, and swapping solo study for a group after repeated weak scores in one subject.

passage:
Week 1, Sunday. Pooja opened her tracking sheet: attendance target 90%, quiz target 60% in each subject. Maths 72, Physics 65, Chemistry 41. She wrote "Chem, watch it" in the margin.
Week 3, Sunday. The sheet told the same story for the third time. Attendance fine everywhere. Maths and Physics above target. Chemistry: 41, 44, 39. Pooja had put in extra solo hours on it every night. Nothing moved. "Doing more of the same isn't working," she wrote.
Week 4, Monday. She messaged Ganga, whose chemistry study group met in the library on Tuesdays and Fridays. "Can I join? I keep failing organic." "Come Tuesday," Ganga replied.
Week 7, Sunday. Chemistry: 58. Still under target, but moving for the first time. Pooja highlighted it in yellow and added a new line: "Keep the group."

qa.q: What were Pooja's chemistry scores in the first three weeks?
How did Pooja feel after three weeks of flat chemistry scores?
qa.a: Pooja felt frustrated and stuck, seeing extra solo hours make no difference.

qa.q: What else could Pooja add to the weekly check?
qa.a: Pooja could note which chemistry topics the group helped with most, so she can ask for help on the next weak area sooner.

qa.q: How might Ganga see Pooja joining the group?
qa.a: Ganga welcomes the request quickly, and Pooja's questions may help the whole group understand organic chemistry better.

grounding: Shows a student checking attendance and scores against targets each Sunday and, after three weeks of weak chemistry scores, swapping solo study for a peer group.

subtype: Approach: tracking weekly progress and adjusting [Revision]
passage: Yash, you're checking your marks every Sunday? Good. Let me tell you what that did for me, back in my second year of college in Darjeeling, after I'd failed two papers. My roommate Pasang made me a simple chart on the back of an old calendar: attendance and quiz scores, every Sunday, against what I'd promised myself. "Tenzin, you have to look even when it's ugly," he said. For three Sundays the chart showed electronics stuck around 40, however many nights I sat alone with the book. On the fourth Sunday I finally admitted it: studying alone wasn't working. There was a group of four who met in the canteen after classes. I asked if I could join. Six weeks later, electronics was at 62. The chart didn't fix anything, Yash. It just stopped me lying to myself.

qa.a: A simple chart on the back of an old calendar.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel on the fourth Sunday?
qa.a: Tenzin felt frustrated but honest, finally admitting that studying alone wasn't working.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the difference?
qa.a: Choosing, after three flat Sundays, to ask the canteen group to join, instead of more nights alone with the book.

qa.q: How did Pasang see the weekly chart?
qa.a: Pasang saw it as a way to face the truth, insisting Tenzin look at it even when it was ugly.

grounding: Illustrates a student tracking weekly scores against targets and, after three weak weeks in one subject, switching from solo study to a peer group.
